title: When Vectors Break Down: Graph-Based RAG for Dense Enterprise Knowledge - Sam Julien, Writer

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is graph-based RAG architecture, knowledge graphs, vector retrieval limitations, and retrieval/search design for enterprise knowledge bases. The talk centers on enterprise search and knowledge-base design for Fortune 500 companies in regulated industries, with enterprise data and workflows as the core context. Writer's graph-based RAG system is deployed in production and benchmarked against seven vector search systems on the RobustQA dataset. The talk assumes familiarity with RAG, embeddings, chunking, and graph databases, and covers advanced techniques like fusion-in-decoder and text-to-graph conversion. Recorded conference presentation delivered at the AI Engineer World's Fair in San Francisco. All thirteen evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript, sourced directly from the transcript.

summary: Sam Julien of Writer outlines the company's multi-year journey building a graph-based RAG system for enterprise customers, particularly in regulated industries like healthcare and finance where accuracy and low hallucination are critical. Enterprise data presents unique challenges: it is dense, specialized, massive (terabytes), and uses clustered, non-diverse language. Writer's evolution progressed from basic keyword search to vector embeddings and chunking, then to graph-based RAG. Vector retrieval failed in two key ways: naive chunking with nearest-neighbor search produced inaccurate answers (e.g., confusing the 1984 Macintosh launch with the 1983 Lisa launch), and it struggled with concentrated data where thousands of documents use identical terms (e.g., a mobile phone company's documents all mentioning megapixels, cameras, battery life), making model comparisons impossible. Graph-based RAG preserved relationships and provided more context, improving accuracy. However, graph databases presented challenges: converting data to structured graphs was costly at scale, Cypher struggled with advanced similarity matching, and LLMs performed better with text-based queries than complex graph structures. Writer's solutions included building a specialized model trained to map data into nodes and edges that runs on CPUs or smaller GPUs, implementing context-aware splitting and chunking, and storing graph data as JSON in a Lucene-based search engine. The team also explored fusion-in-decoder, a technique processing passages independently in the encoder for linear scaling then jointly in the decoder for better evidence aggregation, and combined it with knowledge graphs for two-stage ranking of passages. This implementation drove down hallucination rates. The team returned to the original RAG paper and discovered it proposed a retriever-generator architecture with sequence-to-sequence models but never discussed prompt context and questions, now the de facto approach. Fusion-in-decoder represents an alternate timeline from that original paper. Benchmarking with Amazon's RobustQA dataset against seven vector search systems showed Writer's graph-based RAG with fusion-in-decoder had the best accuracy and fastest response time. Customer benefits include exposing the thought process via snippets, subqueries, and sources; handling multi-hop questions across multiple documents and topics; and managing complex data formats where answers span multiple pages. Three meta lessons emerge: focus on customer problems rather than specific solutions, stay flexible based on team expertise, and let research challenge assumptions.

sections.title: Introduction and Market Context
sections.summary: Sam Julien introduces the talk, noting the market is recognizing vector search alone is insufficient for RAG at scale. Writer is an end-to-end agentic platform building its own models and graph-based RAG system for Fortune 500 and global 2000 companies in regulated industries.

sections.title: Writer's Research Team and Problem Statement
sections.summary: Writer's research team focuses on four areas: enterprise models (Palmyra X5), practical evaluations (failsafe QA), domain-specific models (Palmyra Med, Palmyra Finn), and retrieval/knowledge integration. The core problem is that enterprise data is dense, specialized, massive (terabytes), and uses clustered non-diverse language.

sections.title: Evolution from Search to Vector to Graph-Based RAG
sections.summary: Writer progressed from basic keyword search to vector embeddings and chunking, then to graph-based RAG. Vector retrieval had two major problems: naive chunking with nearest-neighbor search produced inaccurate answers (Apple timeline example), and it failed with concentrated data where thousands of documents use identical terms (mobile phone company example).

sections.title: Graph Database Challenges and Solutions
sections.summary: Graph databases presented four challenges: costly data conversion at scale, Cypher limitations with similarity matching, LLMs preferring text-based queries, and scaling hitting team expertise limits. Solutions included building a specialized model to map text to graph structures running on CPUs/small GPUs, context-aware splitting and chunking, and storing graph data as JSON in a Lucene-based search engine.

sections.title: Meta Lessons and Research Deep Dive
sections.summary: Three meta lessons emerge: focus on customer problems not specific solutions, stay flexible based on team expertise, and let research challenge assumptions. The team returned to the original RAG paper and discovered it never discussed using prompt context and questions, now the de facto RAG approach.

sections.title: Fusion-in-Decoder and Knowledge Graph Integration
sections.summary: The original RAG paper proposed a retriever-generator architecture with sequence-to-sequence models but never discussed prompt context and questions. Fusion-in-decoder processes passages independently in the encoder for linear scaling then jointly in the decoder for better evidence aggregation. Knowledge graph with fusion-in-decoder uses graphs to understand relationships between retrieved passages, enabling two-stage ranking that improves efficiency and lowers cost. Writer built their own fusion-in-decoder implementation, which significantly reduced hallucination rates.

sections.title: Benchmarking Results and Customer Benefits
sections.summary: Writer benchmarked against Amazon's RobustQA dataset, comparing their knowledge graph + fusion-in-decoder system with seven vector search systems, achieving the best accuracy and fastest response time. Customer benefits include exposing the thought process (snippets, subqueries, sources), handling multi-hop questions across multiple documents and topics, and managing complex data formats where answers span multiple pages. Julien emphasizes there are many paths to knowledge graph benefits in RAG—graph databases, creative Postgres usage, or search engines—and reiterates the three meta lessons before noting Writer is hiring.
